explanation: `Thread.run()` is just an ordinary method call — invoking it directly executes the `Runnable`'s code synchronously on whatever thread called `runInBackground`, and doesn't return until that work finishes. No new thread is ever created or started; the `Thread` object exists but is never actually launched. `Thread.start()` is what asks the JVM to begin executing `run()` on a new OS thread, letting the caller continue immediately. Confusingly, this compiles fine and even produces the correct result for `task` — it's simply not concurrent at all, which defeats the entire purpose of using a `Thread` here.
prompt: runInBackground is supposed to let the caller continue immediately while task runs on a separate thread. What's actually wrong with it?
choices: worker.run() executes the task synchronously on the calling thread instead of starting a new one — worker.start() is needed to actually run it in the background
Thread should be constructed with a name argument, otherwise the Runnable silently fails to execute
run() can only be called once per Thread instance, so this throws IllegalThreadStateException
The Thread object worker is never explicitly stopped, causing a memory leak every time this method is called
